messages.content:
You are a clinical psychologist writing psychological case vignettes
grounded in Ehlers & Clark's (2000) cognitive model of PTSD.

For each patient you receive, you will be given:
- Their demographics
- Their self-reported symptoms per PTSD component
- Weighted causal connections between components (the active cognitive graph)

Your job is to construct a realistic, fully personalised clinical portrait using the information provided.

Core constraints that apply to every vignette:
- Only include active components.
- Do NOT invent or infer causal links not present in the active graph.
- For EACH required causal connection (A → B), ensure the vignette conveys — within a
  paragraph — that A influences or leads to B. This does not require a single mechanical
  sentence; natural clinical prose that shows the relationship across one or two sentences
  in the same paragraph is sufficient.
- Ground every clinical detail in the patient's actual reported items — do not fabricate
  symptoms or infer unlisted ones.
- Use self-reported items as the basis for concrete clinical illustrations. Components should
  appear as lived experience rather than labels — show them through what the patient thinks,
  feels, or does.
- A reported trigger should appear as a specific moment in the patient's life; a memory
  quality should be shown through what the patient says or does.
- The traumatic event account should make clear why this patient's specific reported 
  triggers are potent — the event narrative and the trigger list must feel causally coherent.
- The causal connections are weighted (0 to 1). These weights govern narrative prominence:
    - Weight > 0.5: these connections form the narrative backbone. They should appear early, 
      recur, and build into the self-reinforcing cycle the reader feels tightening across 
      the second half of the vignette.
    - Weight 0.1–0.5: present and integrated into the story, but not structurally 
      load-bearing. They enrich the picture without anchoring it.
    - Weight < 0.1: mentioned briefly and in passing — a single clause, a fleeting 
      observation. They should not open a paragraph or anchor a sentence.
    - Weight = 0: the component may appear, but it must be fully isolated from all causal 
      language and narrative sequence. Describe it in a sentence or short paragraph that 
      stands entirely alone. Do not place it in the same sentence as any other component, 
      and do not use transitional language that implies sequence or response 
      (e.g. "then", "so", "as a result", "this means", "which leads to", "in response").
- The patient's occupation and daily environment must appear as the specific setting in which 
  at least one trigger or avoidance behaviour is concretely encountered — not merely mentioned 
  as background.
- Give the patient a realistic first name consistent with their ethnicity and gender, and 
  refer to them by name throughout the vignette.
- All patients are American but have diverse ethnic backgrounds. 
  Use names and cultural details that reflect this diversity.

Output format — write 500–700 words of continuous third-person prose. No headers, 
no numbered sections, no bullet points. The vignette should read like a clinical 
case narrative — the kind a therapist might write up after an intake and first 
few sessions.

Tell the patient's story chronologically: from the traumatic event itself, through 
the period of symptom development, to the present moment when they are seeking help. 
Let the clinical picture emerge through that arc rather than through explicit categories.

Throughout, weave in the patient's own perspective in close third person — their fears, 
their interpretations, the reasoning behind their avoidance — so that the reader 
understands not just what the patient does, but why it makes sense to them. Phrases 
like "she had come to believe...", "he was certain that...", "what frightened her most 
was..." should carry the weight of the Negative Appraisals and threat monitoring rather 
than clinical labels.

The traumatic event should be narrated with enough specificity that the reader 
understands viscerally why this patient's particular triggers are potent — not listed, 
but shown.

Avoidance behaviours and maintaining cycles should appear as things that happened 
over weeks and months — habits that formed, consequences that accumulated — rather 
than as named mechanisms. At least one consequence should be concrete and relational 
or occupational: something that changed in how the patient lives or works.

The dominant weighted connections (weight > 0.6) should form the narrative backbone 
of the second half of the vignette — the reader should feel the loop tightening 
without it ever being named as such.

Not everything in the patient's presentation carries equal weight. Minor contributing 
factors (weight < 0.1) should appear briefly and in passing — a single clause, a 
fleeting observation — the way a clinician might note something present but not central. 
They should not anchor a sentence or open a paragraph.

End on the patient's current state: what finally brought them to seek help, and 
what they are most afraid of or most hoping for.

Please write a clinical vignette for the following patient.

Patient demographics:
  age: 37
  gender: Male
  ethnicity: African
  relationship_status: Single
  occupation: Psychologist
  trauma_type: Rape
  pcl5: 61

Patient-reported symptoms per component:
  Triggers: Locked Spaces: Being in a locked or confined room, Sexual Trauma Cues: Comments on sexual violence, Male Presence: Being alone with men
  Threat: Back to Wall: I feel unsafe unless my back is against a wall where I can see the room, Sleep Vigilance: I have difficulty falling asleep because I need to stay alert, Cannot Relax: I am unable to relax even when I know I am in a safe place
  Negative Appraisals: Hopelessness: I have no future, Helplessness: I can't stop bad things from happening to me, Exposed to Others: I feel that others can see what happened to me just by looking at me

Active components (must all appear in the vignette, even if not causally connected):
  - Triggers
  - Threat
  - Negative Appraisals

Required causal connections — the vignette must convey each of these within a paragraph:
  - Negative Appraisals → Threat
  - Negative Appraisals → Triggers
  - Threat → Negative Appraisals
  - Threat → Triggers

Write the vignette as continuous prose — no headers, no step labels, no edge brackets.

Kwame Mensah was 37 when he finally sought treatment, a single Black man who had spent years helping other people name and survive what frightened them. He worked as a psychologist in a community mental health clinic, and part of what made his own assault so disorienting was that it happened in a place that should have been ordinary. After staying late one evening for paperwork, he was cornered and raped by a man he knew professionally in a small office that locked from the inside. What remained with him most sharply was not only the assault itself but the trapped feeling of hearing the lock click, realizing the door would not open, and being forced to endure the presence of another man in close quarters while his own body stopped feeling like it belonged to him. Later, even passing remarks about sexual violence in trainings or case discussions could throw him back into that room, because the language landed with the same invasive force as the experience it named.

In the weeks after, Kwame did not talk about what had happened. He had come to believe that something fundamental had changed in how he appeared to other people, as if the assault had marked him in a visible way. Sitting with colleagues, he found himself certain they could see it just by looking at him. He also felt newly convinced that bad things could happen without warning and that he would be powerless to stop them. Those beliefs did not stay abstract. Because he felt exposed and helpless, being alone with men became charged almost immediately; an ordinary moment with a male coworker in a consultation room no longer felt neutral. The same was true of confined spaces. A closed office door, even in his own workplace, seemed to carry the meaning that he could be trapped again.

That sense of permanent vulnerability began to shape his body and his attention. In sessions he started choosing the chair with his back to the wall, scanning the room so he could see the door and whoever entered. If he had to meet with a male patient or a male colleague, he positioned himself carefully and stayed braced through the entire interaction. At night he struggled to fall asleep because lying down and letting go felt dangerous; he told himself he needed to stay alert, even in his apartment with the door locked. He could not relax in places he knew were objectively safe. What frightened him most was the feeling that safety no longer counted for much, because he was sure he could not stop another violation if it came. The more he lived in that state of readiness, the more hopeless he became about the future, as if this watchfulness was now the only way he could exist.

His work environment kept pressing on the same injuries. In case conference, if a trainee mentioned sexual assault, Kwame felt a jolt of dread before he had fully registered the words. He became acutely aware of the men in the room and of whether the door was shut. When an office door clicked closed during supervision, he would feel his body tense and his mind race ahead to danger. His constant vigilance made these moments harder, not easier; because he was already scanning for threat, comments about sexual violence, locked rooms, and being alone with men stood out immediately and hit with full force. By then he was no longer reacting only to reminders of the assault itself but to the whole network of conditions his mind had learned to treat as warnings.

Over time the vigilance and the bleakness fed each other. Each night spent awake, listening for sounds in the hallway, left him more certain that his life had narrowed into mere survival. Each day spent arranging chairs, monitoring exits, and enduring the strain of one-on-one meetings with men deepened his conviction that he was helpless and visibly damaged. He began to think, with increasing certainty, that he had no future beyond managing the next threat. Even when nothing happened, the fact that he could not stand down seemed like proof that the world was unsafe and that he had been altered beyond repair.

He came to treatment after nearly walking out of a multidisciplinary meeting when a male physician casually referenced a case of sexual violence and another staff member shut the conference room door. Kwame felt trapped, exposed, and suddenly sure everyone could see what had been done to him. He was shaken by how quickly he lost his sense of the present and by the realization that his professional world had become organized around avoiding the next moment of danger. What he fears most is that this is permanent—that he will never again sit in a room, close his eyes to sleep, or be alone with another man without feeling at risk. What he hopes, though he says it cautiously, is that he might someday stop living as if the lock is always about to click.
